source.title: RoboJEPA: Scaling Robotic Latent World Models
source.authors: Artem Zholus; Nicolas Beltran-Velez; Jianhao Yuan; Sarath Chandar; Tushar Nagarajan; Daniel Severo; Koustuv Sinha; Michal Drozdzal; Adriana Romero Soriano; Jeannette Bohg; Nicolas Ballas; Mahmoud Assran

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests scaling behavior in robotic world models and refines the claim by comparing curve forms and training schedules. Its results show that extrapolation and downstream trends depend on these choices; it is a different setting and measure from language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper measures latent rollout L1 error and robotic planning performance for RoboJEPA, not language-model held-out cross-entropy. It tests scaling in a robotic modality (V5), downstream planning predictability (V6), and dependence on curve fitting and training setup (V7). Cited results from other papers, including the encoder benchmark results in Appendix K, are not recorded as study results. Qualitative decoded-rollout comparisons are not rows because they do not report the scaling measures catalogued here.
record.test_reason: The study fits scaling laws to held-out latent rollout L1 error of robotic world models (22M–8B) against training compute. It also tests whether downstream planning improves predictably with compute, and it compares curve forms and training recipes. Its own results bear on V5 (a new modality), V6 (downstream predictability) and V7 (dependence on fit form and recipe). This is a new setting rather than a direct challenge, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that rollout L1 error follows a second-order power law in compute, which extrapolates better than the standard power law, BNSL or UNSL. They conclude that downstream planning improves predictably with compute and tracks offline error. They find that capabilities emerge at task-specific compute thresholds, and that a long-horizon, higher-resolution cooldown improves high-compute scaling and long-horizon planning. They also note the fits sit near data saturation and cover only the predictor on a frozen encoder.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains robotic latent world models and measures held-out latent rollout L1 error and planning rewards, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. It fits error against total training compute on a compute-optimal frontier, with a frozen encoder and a fixed corpus; it does not reproduce the original language-model parameter/data/compute sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The chosen curve form affects held-out extrapolation error: the second-order power law outperforms the standard first-order law in the reported comparisons. Changing cooldown training from K=2 at 240×320 to K=10 with mixed 240×320 and 480×640 changes fitted curves, rollout error floors, and long-horizon planning outcomes.
record.problems: The scaling laws characterize a predictor on top of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, not joint encoder-predictor scaling. Data come from a fixed corpus trained for multiple epochs and the authors say the fits are close to data saturation. The curve comparison uses a particular fit protocol and setup; no uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling-law extrapolation errors. Downstream RoboCasa curves are shown in figures without tabulated numeric values, and real-robot per-model task results fluctuate across sizes.
record.rows_left_out: None of the retained rows exceed the 60-row limit. Cited results in Appendix K and qualitative decoded-rollout filmstrips in Figures 2, 4, and 12–19 were not extracted as scaling-law or downstream-performance rows.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling in parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of language-model loss. The robotic extrapolation (fit on 22M–2B, test on 4B/8B) spans only about 2–4x in parameters, not orders of magnitude, and is recorded under V5.
There is no fitted parameter/token allocation law. The paper only notes that no model size lies on the frontier entirely.
No controlled shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Image/video generative loss, repeated data, fine-tuning/transfer, and separate laws in N and D. Only the compute-frontier law for a predictor on a frozen encoder is tested.
Language-model downstream tasks. No quantitative correlation between offline loss and planning success is reported.
Parameter counting, data choice, and fitting method beyond the four candidate forms.

missing.what: First-order and second-order fitted parameters from the 22M–2B fit, e.g. α=−0.151 (DROID), −0.103 (RoboCasa) for the first-order law; E=0.218, α=1.91, γ=0.02308 for the second-order DROID fit
Combined DROID+RoboCasa fits for each recipe: short-horizon L=0.194+1.0e-16·C^(1.69−0.0204 lnC); long-horizon L=0.185+4.8e-24·C^(2.40−0.0279 lnC)
Irreducible error close to the observed floor (about 0.2 DROID, 0.17 RoboCasa); authors say the fits are near data saturation
Claim that imagination error strongly correlates with planning, stated without a correlation statistic

record.verdict_notes: V5 is credited for a new modality (robotic latent dynamics) with an L1 loss on frozen-encoder features, not a likelihood. The extrapolation test spans only about 2–4x in parameters (about one order of magnitude in compute), so it says little about V2-style many-orders extrapolation. Downstream frontiers use a tuned stochastic upper-envelope selection with a per-task threshold k (Appendix J.5), a choice that affects how predictable V6 looks. Real-robot results use 30 episodes per cell with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of language-model held-out cross-entropy from smaller to larger language-model runs.
A fitted compute-optimal parameter-count/token-count allocation law; the paper selects a model-size frontier but does not fit growth laws for both parameters and tokens.
Controlled comparisons of architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests robotic latent-world-model rollout L1 against training compute, not image/video generative-model loss, repeated-data language-model training, fine-tuning or transfer of language-model loss laws, or separate scaling in parameters and tokens.
Tests robotic planning performance against compute and relates it to world-model prediction error; does not test language-model downstream tasks.

Shows dependence on fitted curve form and rollout-training recipe in this robotic setup, but does not test language-model parameter-count conventions, alternative language-model datasets, or language-model fitting methods.

relationships.condition: Robotic latent world models, DROID and RoboCasa holdouts, curved (second-order) power law on the compute frontier
relationships.reason: The curved power law fits the frontier and extrapolates to 4B/8B with errors of 0.6 and 1.4 ×10⁻³ (R3, R4). Fitted laws hold for both cooldown recipes (R9–R12).
relationships.display_finding: The curved power law extrapolated to 4B and 8B models with errors of 0.6×10⁻³ and 1.4×10⁻³, respectively, and fitted laws held under both cooldown recipes.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Robotic latent world models, DROID and RoboCasa holdouts, curved (second-order) power law on the compute frontier
source_check.reason: R3–R4 and R9–R12 establish a curved scaling relation with a compute-dependent exponent. This qualifies V5's same power-law form rather than establishing the constant-exponent form.

relationships.reason: The plain power-law form extrapolates 2–3x worse (2.0 and 3.7 ×10⁻³) than the form with an ln C term, so the 'same form' needs a curvature term here (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: The constant-exponent form extrapolated 2–3× worse, with errors of 2.0×10⁻³ and 3.7×10⁻³, than the form incorporating a log-compute term.

source_check.label: limits_scope
